pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 25. Bowls sold: 66. Shrimp caught: 2. Prize won: one pink plastic whistle.*

Ma caught my wrist at the door, still wearing her dental clinic lanyard, which meant she had been working late. "You are moving like a machine," she said. "Machines need rest." I protested that the pot needed watching and the ledger needed counting, but Ma pointed a finger down the market lane. "Go. Play. It is Saturday. The shrimp are not going anywhere."

So I went to the games, and Hui-Ting, who had been sitting on a stool drinking cold lemonade, stood up and came with me. The end of the lane is loud, with Old Mr. Gao standing behind a big square tank of water that glows under strings of tiny light bulbs. Next to him is a ring toss game where the red and yellow rings look exactly one millimeter too small for the glass bottles, which is a beautiful trap.

I watched a boy try, throwing a ring that hit the bottle and bounced off, then another that hit the ground. "Easy," I said. Hui-Ting looked at me, then at the ring. "It looks heavy," she said. I wanted to prove her wrong, so I picked one up. It felt light, but my hand was shaking a little because I was too busy thinking about the angle to care about the weight.
pages.image: Lin and Hui-Ting stand at a night market game stall, staring at a ring toss board with red and yellow plastic rings next to glass bottles, while a boy in the background looks disappointed.

pages.text:
Out of nowhere, Jun appeared. He was loud, as usual, and his spiky hair looked like he had just won an argument with a brush.

"Research," he announced, pointing at the shrimp tank. "My teacher said I need to observe aquatic life in a commercial setting."

"You want to catch shrimp," I said.

"Correct," said Jun. He looked at Hui-Ting. "Is this your thing? You look like you know how to do this."

Hui-Ting shrugged. She always shrugs. It is her way of saying she is not sure if she wants to be there.

We rented three rods. They were blue plastic, and they smelled like old fish. Mr. Gao handed us our tickets.

Hui-Ting did not move. She just waited. Five seconds passed, then ten. A shrimp, bright pink and fuzzy, bumped against her bait. She lifted the rod. One catch.

She tried again. Another shrimp. Two catches. She did not look excited. She just looked tired.

I moved my rod left and right. I splashed water. I almost caught a shoe.

Jun tried to be smooth. He flicked the rod. The line went high. Then it went low. It wrapped around his own sleeve.

"Oops," said Jun.
pages.image: Three children stand at a glowing water tank with fishing rods, one girl holding a caught pink shrimp, a boy tangled in his own line, and Lin looking frustrated, surrounded by colorful market lights.

pages.text:
Mr. Gao took the two shrimp from Hui-Ting and placed them on a small black grill, where the salt hissed and sent up a cloud of sweet smoke. We stood there waiting, watching the flesh turn pink and crisp, and it felt like the longest commercial break in history.

When they were ready, Mr. Gao handed them over. Two halves. One for each of us. Jun ate his half with his eyes closed, chewing slowly as if he was trying to memorize the flavor for a report.

"Good?" I asked.

"Yeah," he said, opening his eyes. "It’s like... fried chicken. But better. And smaller."

Then he stopped chewing. He looked at the grill, then at the water, then at me.

"My dad had a stall here," he said quietly. "Fried chicken. Corner of the lane. Until last year."

He said "closed" like a word he was trying not to touch, similar to how you handle a hot pan you forgot you were holding. The lane was still loud around us, with balloons popping and someone laughing, but the air between us got quiet.

"I’m sorry," I said.

Jun shrugged. "It’s fine. It’s just... different now."
pages.image: Jun stands at a small grill holding a grilled shrimp, his eyes closed, while Lin and Hui-Ting watch him in the background, the water tank glowing behind them.

pages.text:
I remembered that time in class, and the memory felt like a cold draft on my neck. I had laughed, and I had laughed hard, because Jun was making a joke and I thought he was the funniest person in the room. I never stopped to ask why he was always so loud, or why the jokes never really stopped.

Now he looked at me, and the air between us went quiet, like the moment before a fire drill.

"You teased me about the soup," he said, his voice flat. "You said I smelled like it. You said it was embarrassing."

My face heated up, a flush of shame rising from my chest to my ears. I wanted to say it was just a joke, but the words felt too small to cover what I had done.

"I was jealous," Jun said, and he did not look away. "Your stall is still open. Mine isn't. That’s why I said it. Because it’s still there, and it smells good, and you’re proud of it."

Hui-Ting didn’t say a word. She just reached into her jacket pocket and pulled out the prize we had won from the ring toss. It was a pink plastic whistle, shiny and new.

She held it out to Jun.

He took it, wiped his mouth on his sleeve, and put the mouthpiece in his teeth.

*PEEP-PREEEP.*

It was a horrible sound, and also a wonderful one. Every stall keeper in the lane turned around. Uncle Feng dropped his spatula with a loud clatter, and Auntie Ping finally stopped scrolling through her phone to stare at us.

Jun grinned. It was the same grin he always wears, but this time, it looked lighter.
pages.image: Jun blows a pink plastic whistle, his eyes wide with a grin, while Lin looks embarrassed and Hui-Ting smiles softly, with market stall keepers in the background turning to look.

pages.text:
We walked home under the still-glowing lanterns, the steam from the beef noodle pot thinning into the cold air as the night settled in.

I kept thinking about Jun’s face, and the specific, quiet way he said the word *closed*, while my own fear of the lane disappearing sat in my stomach like a wet sock.

Shame is a strange thing to wear. From the outside, it just looks like a kid who is a little bit too quiet, but from the inside it feels like a heavy coat that will not come off.

I reached into my jacket pocket and found the crumpled paper, my redesign with the clean, modern logo and the "Chen Ama’s" written in a font that looked like it came from a website.

Holding it up under the soft yellow streetlamp, I stared at the lines for a long time, though I did not throw it away.

I was not ready for that, so I simply put it back in my pocket, where it felt different now.

Not lighter, just more real.
pages.image: Lin stands under a yellow streetlamp at night, looking down at a crumpled piece of paper in her hand, the night market lane blurred in the background with glowing lanterns.
